newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: U.S., Japan remain 'far apart' in insurance talks.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan remain 'far apart' in insurance talks.

text.p: Japan and the United States remain sharply divided in negotiations to reach an agreement on deregulating Japan's insurance market, acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said Monday.
"I believe we remain very far apart," Barshefsky told a news conference at the World Trade Organisation's first ministerial conference in Singapore.
The United States and Japan have been negotiating since last week to resolve their dispute over changes in Japan's insurance market before a self-imposed Sunday deadline.

Barshefsky said U.S. negotiator Ira Shapiro would be coming to Singapore from Tokyo later Monday and she would decide sometime later whether to return to Tokyo herself for further talks after the WTO meeting ends Friday.
"I would say that going back to Tokyo does frankly not necessarily indicate either that we think there will be an agreement or that there won't," Barshefsky.
The dispute centres on U.S. charges that Japan is planning to renege on a 1994 trade agreement on the deregulation of its $400 billion insurance market.

Washington has argued that the agreement calls for Tokyo to deregulate the huge primary life and casualty insurance sector, which is dominated by Japanese companies, before unleashing competition in the small speciality insurance market. The niche market is the only one in which foreign insurance groups have a firm foothold.

Barshefsky's comments followed remarks by Japan's Vice Finance Minister Tadashi Ogawa, who said in Tokyo Monday that Japan wants the United States to be more flexible in negotiations on their bilateral insurance dispute.
"Japanese and U.S. negotiators are determined to reach an agreement by the deadline. We want to see further flexibility on the part of the U.S.," Ogawa said.
If Barshefsky returns to Tokyo, she will meet Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka Saturday to discuss the issue before the Sunday deadline.
Separately, a Japanese Finance Ministry official said Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the ministry's international finance bureau, and Shapiro will meet again Thursday and Friday.
Sakakibara and Shapiro held talks Sunday and Monday, after Mitsuzuka and Barshefsky failed Friday to bridge wide differences in their talks.
"We have deepened our understanding of each other's position, but differences that the ministers could not narrow in their latest talks still exist," the official said.
"Negotiations are going to be very hard," he said.
